sources.locator: CS2023 Algorithmic Foundations; August 2023; material applicable to Monotonic stack and queue
sources.claim: A monotonic stack or deque removes candidates that cannot be the next greater, smaller, minimum, or maximum answer.

canonicalExplanation.summary: A **monotonic stack** keeps only the items that could still be an answer, in increasing or decreasing order. For **next greater element**: scan left to right, keeping indexes whose next greater value hasn't been found. When a new value arrives, it **resolves** every smaller value on top of the stack (pop them and record the answer), then gets pushed itself. Items that can never be an answer are **thrown away**, which is why the stack doesn't hold every element. Each index is pushed and popped at most once: **O(n)**. A **monotonic deque** does the same for sliding-window maximum or minimum.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A progress page shows, for each day's quiz score, how many days until a higher score. Comparing each day with every later day is O(n²) for a year of scores. A next-greater stack pops smaller values when a new greater value resolves them. In this lesson you'll implement and explain a next-greater or range-extreme problem with a monotonic structure.


sections.heading: The invariant: the stack holds unresolved indexes, values decreasing
sections.body:
```python
def days_until_higher(scores):            # O(n) time, O(n) space.
    answer = [0] * len(scores)            # 0 = never higher.
    stack = []                            # indexes; their scores decrease from bottom to top.
    for i, s in enumerate(scores):
        while stack and scores[stack[-1]] < s:   # s resolves smaller waiting days.
            j = stack.pop()
            answer[j] = i - j
        stack.append(i)                   # i now waits for its own higher score.
    return answer

print(days_until_higher([60, 55, 70, 65, 80, 40]))   # [2, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0]
```

| Question | Structure | Keep |
|---|---|---|
| next greater to the right. | stack, decreasing values. | unresolved indexes. |
| next smaller to the right. | stack, increasing values. | unresolved indexes. |
| max of each window. | deque, decreasing values. | indexes still in the window. |
| min of each window. | deque, increasing values. | indexes still in the window. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why store indexes instead of scores?", "answer": "The answer is a distance (i - j), and windows need to know when an index has expired. Indexes carry both position and, via scores[j], the value."}
```

examples.title: When will my score next go up?
examples.situation: A next-greater stack pops smaller values when a new greater value resolves them.
walkthrough: **Waiting days:** after 60 and 55, the stack holds both, since neither has seen a higher score.
**Pops smaller values when a greater value resolves them:** 70 pops 55 (answer 1 day) and 60 (answer 2 days), then waits itself.
**Test:** [60, 55, 70, 65, 80, 40] will give [2, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0], matching a brute-force double loop on random inputs.
examples.result: The progress page shows every day's wait in one pass over a year of scores.

examples.title: The stock-style span
examples.situation: A streak widget shows, for each day, how many consecutive days up to today had a score no higher than today's.
walkthrough: That's "previous greater" instead of next greater.
Keep a stack of indexes with decreasing scores; pop while the top is ≤ today's score.
The span is today's index minus the index left on top (or i + 1 if the stack is empty).
examples.result: Streak spans are computed in O(n) for any number of days.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A monotonic stack must contain every previously visited element.
misconceptions.correction: It deliberately discards elements that are dominated: once a larger later value appears, smaller earlier values can never be anyone's next greater. Keeping only live candidates is the whole trick.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, what happened to dominated elements?

analogy.example: A monotonic stack is like **people waiting in a queue to see over a wall**: when a taller person arrives, everyone shorter in front of them in line **finally sees someone taller** and leaves. Shorter people never block a taller person's view, so they're safely forgotten.
usefulFor: remembering taller arrivals resolve shorter waiters
discard = they can never be the answer again
limitations: Real queues are first-come; this one resolves from the most recent.
Each person arrives once and leaves once: O(n).

remediation.explanation: Ask two questions: **Which earlier items can never be an answer once this new item arrives?** Pop those. **What order does that leave on the stack?** That's your monotonic direction.

recap.summary: To implement and explain a next-greater or range-extreme problem, keep a monotonic stack (or deque for windows) of unresolved indexes, pop smaller values when a greater one resolves them, record their answers, and push the new index; dominated items can never be answers, so each index is pushed and popped once, giving O(n).
